We can therefore see two closely connected meanings in the changes taking place at this time.
First, they show that the old primitive tribal structure was beginning to break down.
Second, they show the first signs, emerging from within the tribal system itself, of the new social order toward which economic development was moving.
These two processes were internally connected. We can see them in the following developments.
As Arabia first took on the role of commercial middleman and then became directly involved in trade, the exchange of useful goods naturally began to take on a more developed economic form.
A measure of exchange value appeared: something against which the value of every item being exchanged could be compared.
Among the people of Arabia during the period we are studying, this measure took two parallel forms.
The first was barter based on one major commodity that effectively served as money.
The second was the more advanced and final form produced by exchange itself: money proper, which Engels called the “commodity of commodities.”
Camels were the main commodity that performed the function of money.
This was because camels occupied such a central place in Bedouin life. Raising them was therefore one of the main forms of productive work in the desert economy.
In Mecca, however, and in the Arab markets drawn into the trading network of Quraysh, exchange was based mainly on metal currency.
Two main coins circulated: the Byzantine gold dinar and the Sasanian silver dirham.

The use of both currencies reflected the different sources of the trade controlled above all by the leaders of Quraysh. They were operating between the two empires that dominated the eastern and western worlds of the time: the Sasanian Persian Empire and the Byzantine Empire.

It seems that Yemeni, or Himyarite, money was also used. This was not minted coinage but pieces of raw gold, either imported from Africa or collected from riverbeds in Yemen. Pieces of raw silver were also used.
These unminted forms of money were exchanged according to their weight.

Whatever form the currency took, the very fact that exchange was increasingly based on money was itself a sign that the tribal system was beginning to break down. Monetary exchange was fundamentally at odds with the communal values of tribal society.
The rise of economic exchange in this form also made trade an important force in the historical transformation we are trying to trace in Arabia.

This does not contradict the scientific principle that the exchange of commodities cannot by itself cause a social system to collapse. At most, exchange can speed up a process of breakdown that has deeper causes.
In other words, exchange cannot be the decisive factor.
The decisive factor is social production itself: the production of the material goods society needs.
Exchange comes after production. If nothing is produced, there is nothing to exchange.
But this does not mean that trade has no effect on development.

We have already seen the two-way relationship between agricultural production and trade in Arabia. Once farming produced more than people needed for their own immediate use, commodity exchange naturally developed and became more active.
Then exchange, in turn, encouraged further growth in productivity, including in handicraft production that had already separated from agriculture.

Primitive communal ownership had been the foundation of tribal society. But the history of pre-Islamic Arabia shows that this foundation was already close to collapse as the sixth century drew to an end and the seventh century began.

By this stage, communal ownership seems to have survived in little more than one form: shared ownership of grazing land and water sources such as wells and springs. Some pastures, wells and springs still appear to have belonged jointly to particular tribes. Reports about pre-Islamic Arabia often describe a place as “the pasture of the camels of such-and-such a tribe” or “the water of such-and-such a tribe.” In other words, they name an entire tribal group as the owner of the place.

But we do not find similar reports describing a particular piece of farmland as the property of a whole tribe or clan. We sometimes hear of herds of camels or other livestock being associated with the name of a tribe or clan. But this does not prove that the herds were collectively owned, because other reports from pre-Islamic Arabia point in the opposite direction. References to camels, horses and sheep owned by individuals are far more common. In the language of legal scholars, these reports therefore qualify the broader wording of the others, where whole herds are simply attached to the names of tribes.

The reports about the many oases scattered across the Arabian Peninsula do not clearly tell us what form agricultural ownership took there. Arab chroniclers do tell us, however, that the people living in these oases were settled rather than nomadic, and that by the late pre-Islamic period they were living in villages and thriving towns with markets for trade. Yathrib, later known as Medina, and al-Ṭāʾif were among these towns.

From the settled way of life in these places, and especially from what we know about Medina and al-Ṭāʾif, we can reasonably conclude that private ownership of land was the dominant form in these oases. We know that communal ownership had no real place in towns such as Medina and al-Ṭāʾif.

As for the other oases, where farming was carried out by partly settled tribal populations, the reports do not tell us clearly whether fields and orchards were owned collectively or privately. The fact that whole groups migrated seasonally away from these oases is not enough, by itself, to prove communal ownership.

But we have already said that we are dealing here with a stage in which handicrafts had separated from agriculture. In other words, production for exchange had begun to develop. The logical conclusion is therefore that society had already moved beyond the stage in which people produced only for their own immediate needs—the stage that went together with primitive communal ownership.
Let us return, then, to the one surviving form of this primitive communal system: shared ownership of grazing land, together with the wells and springs connected to it.

Even this last form was now shrinking and moving toward disappearance. Tribal chiefs had begun to own large numbers of camels privately, and they increasingly reserved these communal resources for the use of their own herds. We also have reports showing that some irrigation waters had already become private property.
This inequality was no longer limited to towns and settled communities. It had become a widespread feature even among the tribes of the desert.

Upper groups were beginning to form around tribal chiefs and their families. They owned large numbers of livestock, especially camels, far more than ordinary members of the tribe. At the same time, some members of the tribe owned nothing at all. The same kind of inequality could also be seen at times in the ownership of slaves.

This difference in wealth allowed tribal chiefs to take control of grazing lands and water sources for their own private benefit. They then created a kind of “legal” justification for this control by claiming a right of priority for themselves as a privileged group.

At this point, inequality was no longer simply a matter of one person owning more personal property than another. The very nature of ownership had changed. What had developed was inequality in the private ownership of the means of production.

Large herds of livestock had become productive assets. Camels, in particular, had acquired the value of commodities. They were used in barter as a standard for measuring the value of other goods and therefore began to perform one of the functions of money.

So when a tribal chief and his close relatives owned large herds, those animals were no longer simply possessions for their own use. Raising them had become a productive activity aimed at exchange. The purpose was to increase income, and as money began to enter local trade, that income increasingly took the form of monetary wealth.

We know that chiefs and their relatives sold livestock beyond what they needed for their own consumption. They sold this surplus in local markets across the Arabian Peninsula, in markets outside Arabia, and along the commercial caravan routes through the desert.

This inequality in private ownership produced unequal standards of living and growing social differences within the tribe itself. The tribe began to divide into rich and poor among its free members, on top of the older division between free people and slaves.
Economic inequality and social division of this kind did not fit the normal workings of the old tribal system. They were therefore clear signs that this system had begun to break down.

The growing distance between the upper and lower groups within the tribe could be seen in many everyday details. Chiefs set up their tents on higher ground overlooking the tents of the rest of the tribe. Their tents were better and more valuable. Their household possessions included expensive rugs and costly metal and glass vessels. They had better weapons and finer saddles for their horses and camels.
A degree of material luxury had entered the lives of the chiefs, while the poor members of the tribe were living in hardship.

The well-known phenomenon of the ṣaʿālīk in this period was a direct result of this economic and social inequality. The ṣaʿālīk were poor men from different tribes who broke away from their tribal communities and lived independently in the desert, supporting themselves through raiding and plunder.
Their break with the tribe expressed two realities that pointed in the same direction.
First, they were rejecting a form of belonging that demanded complete attachment to tribal life and obedience to its rules and customs, however much poverty or oppression they suffered.
Second, their departure reflected a material need that had become unbearable within the tribe itself.

The significance is clear. Social inequality had begun to affect the weaker sections of the tribe so deeply that some of them were driven to break their tribal ties altogether. This was itself another sign that the tribal system was beginning to come apart from within.

The way people made a living was changing. It was moving away from the old primitive communal form and toward a more individual form, because ownership of the means of subsistence and production was also changing.
These economic changes, in turn, changed the social structure of tribal society in pre-Islamic Arabia.

One of the clearest changes appeared in the bonds that held tribal unions together. During the late pre-Islamic period, blood and descent were no longer the only basis for forming these larger groups. Two new kinds of relationship were added: walāʾ, or affiliation, and formal alliance.

Walāʾ meant that “an individual, clan, subclan, or tribe attached itself to another tribe. They became its clients and broke their ties with their former tribe. This was not the same as the walāʾ of slavery or servitude (...) These clients had all the rights enjoyed by members of the tribe.”
The second kind of relationship was alliance. Two or more tribes could form an alliance because they shared interests, whether immediate or long-term.

One example was the alliance that al-Muṭṭalib arranged between Quraysh and al-Aḥābīsh. Another was the alliance between the tribes of ʿĀmila, Judhām and Lakhm. Jawād ʿAlī rightly concludes that this alliance arose “from common interests and similar circumstances that brought them together, as we have seen with other tribes, until with the passing of time it came to be treated as a relationship of descent.”

There was also a form of alliance in which weaker tribes became attached to stronger ones, until the whole alliance came to be known by the name of its strongest member. Arab chroniclers called this iṭfāʾ. They say, for example, that Ḍabba was “absorbed” when it allied with al-Ribāb, that al-Ḥārith was absorbed when it allied with Madhḥij, and that ʿAbs was also absorbed when it moved to Banū ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿa on the day of Jabala.

Perhaps the description that comes closest to the actual nature of these alliances, and to their historical and social meaning, is the one Herodotus, the Greek historian, gave to the idea of the tribe in the fifth century AD. He said that a tribe was not simply an alliance based on descent or kinship. It was also a political union.
That is the main point we should draw from the spread of tribal alliances in late pre-Islamic Arabia.

The pure bond of blood and descent was beginning to weaken. The reason was that the old system of primitive communal ownership was breaking down, while private ownership of the means of production in the desert was emerging. This produced growing differences in living standards among members of the same tribe and created new forms of social inequality.

Herodotus, however, could not uncover the economic and social causes behind this kind of “political union.” He therefore treated it as part of the original meaning of the tribe itself. But the tribe had originally been based on blood and descent. Only later did that begin to change.
The rise of private ownership of livestock among the tribes of late pre-Islamic Arabia also changed the form of exchange in the desert economy.
Exchange was no longer mainly carried out between one tribe and another as two collective units. It increasingly took place between individuals, both within the tribe and outside it.
This new form of exchange clearly shows that the unity of the tribe was beginning to break down. The tribal system had lost its old material foundation: communal ownership.

We do not lack evidence that individual exchange had become the common form during this period. Quite the opposite. What we would now have to search for is evidence that the older form—collective exchange—still survived. Such evidence is absent from the reports we have about this period.

And if this was true of the desert economy, it was even more true of agricultural and craft products. Exchange in these goods belonged to the settled or partly settled economy, which had moved even further away than the nomadic economy from the old communal relations of exchange.
It is true that markets throughout the Arabian Peninsula were supervised by tribal chiefs, especially those who called themselves “kings” in imitation of the Arab kings of al-Ḥīra and the Ghassānids.

The chief of Dūmat al-Jandal, for example, called himself a king. So did the chiefs of Taymāʾ from Banū ʿAbd Allāh ibn Zayd. These chiefs began to act like kings by imposing a ten-percent tax on merchants using the markets under their control.

But their supervision of these markets did not mean that they conducted trade on behalf of their tribes as a whole. They were not collectively selling the tribe’s production in exchange for goods that would belong to the whole tribe.
This kind of collective exchange no longer existed.
First, there was no longer collective ownership of the tribe’s production.

Second, the chiefs did not supervise the markets in order to organize communal exchange. Their purpose was to create the administrative conditions that allowed them to increase their own private wealth. They collected the ten-percent tax from market traders. They collected tribute from tribes under their control and treated it as part of their personal income. They also charged merchants for allowing caravans to pass through their territories and for providing those caravans with protection.
Third, these chiefs were themselves merchants. They sent their own goods to markets elsewhere, just as the kings of al-Ḥīra and the wealthy merchants of Mecca did.
During the period we are studying, the authority of a tribal or clan chief no longer drew its strength from tribal custom alone.

Increasingly, the chief’s authority depended on his economic position. A man who possessed enough wealth could defeat his rivals and gain influence over members of the tribe by providing material benefits and services that affected their daily lives.
This is why tribal chiefs became increasingly concerned with accumulating wealth by every means available to them.

They expanded their private ownership of the means of production, both in the desert and in settled areas. They increased their commercial activity in markets inside Arabia and beyond it. They collected tribute and taxes imposed by force on tribes, merchants and caravans.
They even used the famous pre-Islamic ideal of generosity to strengthen their authority.
Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī, whose generosity became proverbial, expressed this clearly when he said:
They tell me, “You have squandered your wealth, so show restraint.” But had I not spent as they say, I would never have been a chief.

Nothing shows more clearly how important wealth had become in pre-Islamic society—sometimes more important than traditional tribal considerations—than two historical incidents mentioned by chroniclers and transmitters of reports.

The first concerns Abū Ṭālib, the Prophet’s uncle. Despite his high standing within Quraysh, he lost the offices of rifāda and siqāya—providing food and water to pilgrims—because of his financial weakness.
The second concerns the conversion to Islam of ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī, as related by al-Dhahabī through Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī, Ibn Sīrīn and Abū ʿUbayda ibn Ḥudhayfa.
According to this report, the Prophet said:
“ʿAdī, accept Islam and you will be safe. I know what prevents you from accepting Islam: the poverty you see among those around me, and the fact that you see all the people united against us.”
“I have not been there, but I know where it is.”
“A woman will soon travel from al-Ḥīra without protection until she circles the House. And the treasures of Kisrā will be opened to us.”
